content.title: About
content.content: Energy drink is a non‑alcoholic beverage enriched with caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and sugar or its substitutes. It is intended to boost alertness, improve concentration and temporarily increase physical endurance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial energy drink appeared in Japan in the 1960s under the brand “Lipovitan”.
A typical energy drink (80‑100 mg caffeine) contains roughly the same amount of caffeine as a strong cup of coffee.
Taurine, often added to these drinks, occurs naturally in meat and fish and helps regulate electrolyte balance.
Many countries restrict the sale of energy drinks to minors by law.
Some brands use natural extracts of guarana or ginseng to enhance the effect.

items.title: Increased alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving attention and reaction time.

items.title: Energy replenishment
items.content: Sugar and glucose polymers quickly restore muscle glycogen, which can be useful during intense workouts.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, B3, B6 and B12 support carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Electrolyte balance
items.content: Some formulas contain sodium and potassium, helping to prevent dehydration.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Caffeine raises dopamine levels, which may temporarily improve mood.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat and increased blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption of high‑sugar drinks raises the risk of tooth decay and obesity.

items.title: Interaction with alcohol
items.content: Mixing energy drinks with alcohol can mask intoxication, increasing the risk of overexertion.

items.title: Not recommended for children and pregnant women
items.content: Due to high caffeine and stimulant levels, these drinks are not advised for children, adolescents, pregnant or nursing women.

items.title: Cardiovascular concerns
items.content: People with heart conditions should limit or avoid energy drinks.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Energy drinks are usually consumed cold, straight from the can. A typical serving is 250‑350 ml (one can) within 1‑2 hours. Do not exceed 2‑3 servings per day and avoid combining with other caffeine sources.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the drink in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 24 hours.
